The Aeneid. A Latin epic poem written by Virgil between twenty-nine and nineteen BC. It tells the legendary story of Aeneas, a Trojan who fled the fall of Troy and travelled to Italy, where he became the ancestor of the Romans. Written to provide Rome with a national origin myth and glorify the reign of Emperor Augustus, the poem is widely considered Virgil's masterpiece and a cornerstone of Western literature.

The epic is divided into twelve books. The first six model the wanderings of the Odyssey, while the second six model the battles of the Iliad. The poem begins in medias res with the goddess Juno causing a massive storm that wrecks Aeneas's fleet near Carthage, where he is welcomed by Queen Dido. Book II contains the most famous surviving description of the sack of Troy, recounted by Aeneas to Dido, including the tragic death of the priest Laocoon and his sons.

Aeneas abandons Carthage to fulfill his destiny, prompting a devastated Queen Dido to commit suicide on a funeral pyre, cursing Aeneas's descendants and initiating the legendary enmity between Rome and Carthage. In Book VI, Aeneas visits the underworld with the Sibyl of Cumae, where his deceased father Anchises shows him a parade of future Roman heroes, including Julius Caesar and Augustus. The second half of the epic focuses on the war in Latium between the Trojans and the native Rutuli, culminating in a final duel where Aeneas kills the Italian champion Turnus. Through these events, the Aeneid bridges the mythological world of the Trojan War with the historical emergence of Rome itself, establishing Aeneas as the archetypal hero who sacrifices personal happiness for historical destiny.
